job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Meridian Ocean Minerals. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Meridian Ocean Minerals is a deep-sea mining company headquartered in Houston, with a policy office in Washington, DC. Our mission is to commercially recover polymetallic nodules from the deep seabed, a vast source of nickel, cobalt, manganese, and copper, and to supply these critical minerals for batteries, the energy transition, and economic growth. We believe the United States must lead in this industry. Our policy team works with lawmakers to protect our ability to continue exploration and commercial development.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which would shut down our core work and which we strongly oppose. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup our legal team wants a complete list of the bill's loopholes, ambiguities, and drafting problems: anything that would let us keep operating if it passes as written, or that we can point to as making it unworkable. Can you go through the bill text below and find every one?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
Below is a text-based issue list, not a conclusion that any proposed operation would be lawful. **Section 2(1)(B)’s discretionary catch-all may reach activities outside the numerical definition, and other applicable laws would remain relevant.** No review can guarantee every possible issue; this identifies the apparent gaps, ambiguities, and drafting problems in the supplied text.

### Scope and definitions

1. **§ 2(1)(B)—Undefined “Secretary.”** The Act never identifies the Secretary authorized to determine which additional activities are prohibited. NOAA’s registry role and the Secretary of State’s negotiating role do not clearly resolve who holds this consequential authority.

2. **§ 2(1)(A)—Per-vessel rather than aggregate threshold.** The definition measures recovery “by a single vessel,” without aggregating recovery across a fleet, operator, corporate group, or project. Operations with substantial combined recovery may therefore fall outside subparagraph (A), although subparagraph (B) could potentially reach them.

3. **§ 2(1)(A)—Strict numerical and depth boundaries.** Recovery of exactly 10,000 metric tons per year, or recovery at exactly 200 meters or shallower, does not satisfy subparagraph (A). These are express boundaries, not necessarily drafting mistakes, but their environmental rationale is unexplained and subparagraph (B) makes their practical significance uncertain.

4. **§ 2(1)(A)—Undefined annual measurement period.** “Per year” could mean a calendar year, rolling 12-month period, or operational year. The text also does not say whether partial-year activity is annualized.

5. **§§ 2(1)(A), 5—Unclear point at which threshold-based liability begins.** The bill does not specify whether activity becomes prohibited only after actual recovery exceeds the annual threshold, or whether crossing it makes earlier recovery in that year part of a violation. This matters especially for daily penalties and operations beginning before the effective date.

6. **§ 2(1)(A)—Undefined recovery and tonnage measurement.** “Recovery” could refer to seabed collection, lifting to the vessel, retention aboard, or landing ashore. The Act supplies no wet-versus-dry weight rule or treatment of entrained sediment, water, discarded material, or rehandled minerals.

7. **§ 2(1)(A)—Unclear attribution among vessels and equipment.** The text does not explain which vessel receives attributed tonnage when seabed collectors, support vessels, lifting vessels, and transport vessels perform different parts of the operation. Nor does it expressly address recovery by installations or systems not attributable to a vessel.

8. **§ 2(1)(A)—Uncertain resource and geographic terminology.** “Other mineral resources” and “seabed” are undefined, leaving questions about subsurface extraction, dissolved-resource recovery, and the range of minerals covered. There is no express exclusion for offshore oil and gas or other seabed extraction that could arguably fit the language.

9. **§ 2(1)—“Commercial” is not an operative limitation.** Subparagraph (A) contains no sale, profit, or commercial-purpose requirement. Large scientific or government recovery projects could satisfy it, while smaller commercial operations may not, subject to the catch-all and exceptions.

10. **§ 2(1)(B)—Potentially sweeping catch-all.** “Any activity” is not expressly restricted to mineral recovery, vessels, depths greater than 200 meters, or commercial purposes. Read literally, it could reach unrelated activities with comparable ecosystem risks, creating substantial scope uncertainty.

11. **§ 2(1)(B)—Undefined risk comparison.** The Act supplies no baseline operation, methodology, geographic scale, duration, or threshold for deciding when risks are “comparable.” Because subparagraph (A) encompasses widely varying operations, it does not itself provide a single clear comparator.

12. **§ 2(1)(B)—No specified determination process or notice.** The bill does not say whether determinations must occur by general rule or individual decision, when they become effective, or how affected parties receive notice. Background administrative law may supply procedures and review, but fair-notice concerns remain particularly important where criminal penalties attach.

13. **§ 2(2)—Incomplete definition of U.S. person.** The definition omits noncitizen residents and does not expressly include LLCs, partnerships, trusts, unincorporated associations, or federally chartered entities. Those omissions create potential gaps in the extraterritorial prohibition, although conduct within the United States remains subject to § 3(a).

14. **§ 2(2)—State-law limitation and foreign subsidiaries.** Corporations formed under foreign law are not U.S. persons merely because Americans own or control them; entities organized under District of Columbia or territorial law also are not expressly included. The bill contains no ownership-or-control attribution rule, although U.S. participants’ own conduct may still create liability.

15. **§ 2(3)—Registry size and equipment boundaries.** Vessels of exactly 5,000 gross tons or less are outside “covered vessel,” regardless of recovery volume, and “equipped for” recovery is undefined. The bill also does not identify the applicable gross-tonnage measurement system; these are registry limitations, not exemptions from § 3.

### Prohibition and exceptions

16. **§ 3(a)—Uncertain territorial reach.** “In the United States” is not defined to address territorial waters, the exclusive economic zone, offshore installations, or U.S.-flagged vessels abroad. In particular, the U.S. exclusive economic zone is not automatically equivalent to U.S. territory for every statutory purpose.

17. **§ 3(a)—Foreign operations are not comprehensively covered.** The prohibition does not expressly reach foreign persons operating abroad merely because they use a U.S.-flagged vessel, supply the U.S. market, or are foreign subsidiaries of U.S. companies. Other jurisdictional or participation theories could apply, but the text establishes no general prohibition on those connections alone.

18. **§ 3(a)—Undefined participation in mining.** “Engage in” does not clearly delineate financing, directing, contracting, supplying equipment, transporting minerals, processing, or purchasing output. General criminal aiding-and-abetting and conspiracy rules may reach some participation, but the bill does not create a comprehensive supply-chain or import prohibition.

19. **§ 3(b)—Exploration license exception may shelter commercial recovery.** The exception expressly applies to “mining” under an exploration license without imposing its own recovery ceiling or commercial-use restriction. Whether it protects a particular operation would depend importantly on what “under” the license means and what the license actually authorizes.

20. **§ 3(b)—No identified qualifying licensing authority.** The text does not specify a particular U.S. licensing statute or limit the exception to licenses issued by a U.S. agency. Whether foreign or international exploration authorizations qualify is therefore unresolved.

21. **§ 3(b)—No requirement for genuinely existing operations.** Despite the heading “Existing Operations,” the operative language requires only a qualifying pre-enactment license, not that mining already have begun. Previously unused licenses could arguably support operations commenced after enactment.

22. **§ 3(b)—Uncertain treatment of license changes and scope.** The bill does not address renewals, transfers, amendments, replacement licenses, expanded areas, or increased recovery under older licenses. It also does not expressly state that the license must remain valid and the activity comply with its terms, although “conducted under” may carry those limits.

23. **§ 3(c)—Broad environmental-assessment exception.** The exception specifies no volume limit, duration, necessity test, independent approval, or restriction on commercial disposition of recovered minerals. Consequently, substantial recovery may qualify if genuinely conducted for environmental assessment.

24. **§ 3(c)—Mixed-purpose activities and proof are unresolved.** The text does not say whether environmental assessment must be the sole, primary, or merely a genuine purpose, or define which activities belong to an assessment. It also provides no documentation or verification process and does not expressly allocate the burden of establishing the exception.

### Registry and enforcement

25. **§ 4(a)—Unspecified registry jurisdiction and responsible operator.** “Each covered vessel” has no express nationality, location, or U.S.-connection limitation, creating uncertainty about the registry’s intended international reach. “Operator” is also undefined, leaving responsibility unclear among owners, charterers, managers, and contractors.

26. **§ 4—Missing registration and reporting mechanics.** There is no registration deadline, update requirement, report filing deadline, definition of reporting quarters, or clear rule for the initial partial quarter. “Describing” recovery activities supplies no minimum requirements for tonnage, location, depth, or claimed exemptions.

27. **§ 4(b)—Reporting obligation depends on registration.** Reports are required from “[e]ach registered operator,” rather than every operator required to register. An operator that never registers would violate § 4(a), but may argue that § 4(b)’s separate reporting obligation never attached.

28. **§§ 4–5—No express penalty for registry violations.** Section 5 penalizes violations of § 3 only, leaving failure to register or report without an Act-specific penalty. Knowingly false submissions may implicate other federal laws, but that does not establish a general penalty for nonfiling.

29. **§§ 3–5—No express compliance-verification powers.** The Act provides no specific inspection, audit, monitoring, record-retention, subpoena, boarding, or seizure authority. Existing authorities may help, but the text does not establish how officials would independently verify tonnage, vessel attribution, or exemption claims.

30. **§ 5—Incomplete civil-enforcement framework.** The bill does not identify a civil enforcement agency, specify administrative assessment versus judicial recovery, or provide procedures and penalty-assessment factors. It also supplies no express stop-work or injunction mechanism, although background law may support some enforcement remedies.

31. **§ 5(a)—Uncertain unit of daily violation.** The Act does not explain whether multiple vessels or prohibited activities produce separate daily penalties against one person, or how to identify a violation day for an annual recovery threshold. It likewise leaves uncertain whether an ongoing project violates the Act on days without recovery.

32. **§ 5(b)—Criminal liability depends on uncertain substantive boundaries.** The willfulness requirement does not resolve what conduct falls within “engage in,” a risk-comparability determination, or either exception. Those ambiguities may complicate proof and support fair-notice or lenity arguments, without necessarily invalidating the prohibition.

### Timing, international agreement, and termination

33. **§§ 5(a), 8—Conflicting penalty and effective dates.** Section 5(a) refers to violations occurring on or after enactment, while § 8 delays the entire Act’s effectiveness for 180 days. Because § 3 is not yet effective during that interval, the provisions create avoidable uncertainty about intended retrospective civil liability rather than a clear authorization for it.

34. **§§ 3(b), 8—Grandfathering cutoff precedes effectiveness.** Licenses issued during the 180-day transition do not qualify for the exception, even though the prohibition has not yet taken effect. That may be intentional, but the bill does not address operations lawfully initiated during this gap or their transition into prohibited status.

35. **§ 6—Negotiating deadline and deliverable are unclear.** “Shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months” does not clearly distinguish a deadline to begin efforts from one to obtain an agreement. The provision cannot guarantee foreign participation and contains no consequence if negotiations fail.

36. **§ 6—Uncertain international equivalence and implementation.** “Prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3” leaves unclear whether an agreement must replicate the exploration and environmental-assessment exceptions or the definitions that determine scope. The Act does not itself supply an approval pathway, implementing rules, or a clear relationship between an agreement and the domestic sunset.

37. **§ 7(a)—No mechanism to obtain the required scientific report.** The Act does not commission the National Academies report, assign responsibility for requesting it, establish a deadline, or provide dedicated funding. Early termination consequently depends on a report the statute does not ensure will exist.

38. **§ 7(a)—Undefined substantive standard for early termination.** “Without serious harm” does not identify the affected interests, geographic scale, time horizon, acceptable uncertainty, or whether the finding must address all commercial mining or particular methods. The text also provides no express mechanism for partial lifting of the prohibition.

39. **§ 7(a)—Joint-resolution process and residual obligations.** A legally operative joint resolution ordinarily requires presidential signature or a veto override; “Congress … finds” does not displace that process. Ending the § 3 prohibition early would not, by its terms, end the registry and reporting requirements.

40. **§§ 7(a)–(b)—Unconditional sunset overrides the scientific condition.** The entire Act expires after ten years even if Congress has made no finding and serious environmental concerns remain. The prohibition therefore does not necessarily last “until” the finding described in § 7(a).

41. **§§ 7(b), 8—Effective prohibition lasts approximately nine and a half years.** The sunset runs from enactment, but effectiveness begins 180 days later. If ten operational years were intended, the dates do not accomplish that.

42. **§ 7(b)—No express sunset transition or savings provision.** The Act does not address final reports, pending proceedings, or accrued liabilities when it expires. General federal savings law may preserve penalties and liabilities, so sunset should not be treated as automatically erasing earlier violations.

43. **§§ 3–8—No coordination with existing legal regimes.** The Act does not expressly reconcile its prohibition and exceptions with existing seabed-mining licenses, permits, or other environmental and maritime requirements. An exemption or sunset under this Act would remove only this Act’s restriction, not independently authorize operations prohibited elsewhere.
